The Obsidian makes sense if you'll use the $100 hotel credit and earn meaningfully on both housing and your 3x category. If you don't pay rent or a mortgage, a Chase Sapphire Preferred is probably the simpler $95 choice — but if you do, the Obsidian has a real edge.

title: Bilt Mastercard Palladium
scouts_verdict: The Bilt Palladium is a legit premium card contender. Flat 2x everywhere with transferable points, $600 in annual credits that beat the $495 fee, Priority Pass for you and two guests, and the only premium card that earns on housing. If you pay rent or a mortgage and want one card to handle everything, the Palladium makes an argument that the Venture X and CSR simply can't.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Bilt Mastercard Palladium is Bilt's premium flagship, and it wants to be your one card for everything. At $495 a year, you get a flat 2x on all everyday spending, up to 1.25x on housing, Priority Pass lounge access with two guests, $400 in hotel credits, $200 in annual Bilt Cash, a concierge, and access to the full Bilt transfer partner lineup. Oh, and you can stack 4% Bilt Cash on top of that 2x. It's a lot.

Here's the pitch in plain English: the Palladium is a Capital One Venture X competitor that also earns on your rent or mortgage. If you're a high spender who wants one premium card that does everything without category micromanagement — and you happen to pay housing — this is the card that was designed for you. The $600 in annual credits exceed the $495 fee before you earn a single point, and the flat 2x earn rate means you never have to think about which card to pull out.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 2x on Everything: Flat-rate earning on every non-housing transaction. No categories, no caps, no mental gymnastics.
  • Up to 1.25x on Housing: Earn on rent, mortgage, and HOA fees with no transaction fees. The Bilt signature move.
  • $400 Bilt Travel Hotel Credit: Two $200 credits per year for qualifying hotel bookings through the Bilt portal. This alone covers most of the fee.
  • $200 Annual Bilt Cash Bonus: Credited upon opening and around January 1st each year. Free money, recurring.
  • Priority Pass + 2 Guests: Unlimited access to 1,400+ lounges. Bring your travel crew.
  • 4% Bilt Cash on Everyday Spending: Stacks on top of the 2x base. Your effective return on everyday spend is genuinely impressive.
  • Full Transfer Partner Access: 1:1 to Hyatt, American Airlines, United, Air Canada, Turkish, Virgin Atlantic, IHG, and more.
  • Dedicated Concierge: White-glove help with travel, dining, and events. The kind of perk that's nice until you actually need it — then it's amazing.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees.
  • World Legend Mastercard: Top-tier protections — cell phone coverage, travel insurance, rental car CDW.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee$495

Rent / Mortgage Payment FeeNone

Let's do the math: $400 hotel credit + $200 Bilt Cash = $600 in guaranteed annual value. The fee is $495. You're $105 ahead before earning a single point, sipping a single lounge coffee, or calling the concierge once. That's not creative accounting — that's just credits exceeding the fee. Straightforward.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 50,000 Bilt Points + Gold Status after spending $4,000 on everyday purchases in the first 90 days, plus $300 in Bilt Cash.

That's a strong package. The 50,000 points are fully transferable — route them through Hyatt at ~2 cents per point and you're looking at up to $1,000 in hotel value. Add the $300 Bilt Cash and first-year credits, and the Palladium pays for itself several times over in year one. Premium card sticker shock, first-year value that more than compensates.

Same formula across all Bilt cards — your housing rate scales with your Everyday Spend Ratio:

  • 25% ratio: 0.5x on housing
  • 50% ratio: 0.75x on housing
  • 75% ratio: 1.0x on housing
  • 100% ratio: 1.25x on housing

The flat 2x on everything is this card's killer feature. No choosing categories, no caps, no rotating quarterly nonsense. Every swipe earns the same. Layer on 4% Bilt Cash and your effective return on everyday spending is well above 2% — and that's before you even consider transfer partner value. For people who hate optimizing and just want one great card, this is the answer.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
• Transfer Partners: 1:1 to American Airlines, United, Hyatt, Air Canada Aeroplan, Turkish Miles&Smiles, Virgin Atlantic, IHG, Hawaiian Airlines, Avianca LifeMiles, and more.
  • Bilt Travel Portal: Book flights and hotels directly.
  • Rent / Mortgage: Apply points toward housing payments. Yes, your credit card rewards can pay your rent.
  • Home Down Payment: Contribute points toward a home purchase through Bilt's Points to a Home program.
  • Fitness and Dining: Redeem at Bilt partner locations.
  • Bilt Cash: Convert to statement credits.

Transfer partners are the highest-value play, always. At 2x earning on everything, you accumulate points fast. Move them to Hyatt for premium stays and you're looking at 4+ cents per dollar spent on everyday purchases. That turns your coffee run, your Amazon order, and your grocery haul into future hotel stays. It's a good system.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• $400 Bilt Travel Hotel Credit: Two $200 credits per year for qualifying Bilt portal hotel bookings.
  • $200 Annual Bilt Cash Bonus: Automatically credited each year. No action needed.
  • Priority Pass + 2 Guests: Unlimited entry at 1,400+ lounges (excluding restaurants). Bring your people.

The Palladium adds housing rewards, more credits ($600 vs. $400), and Bilt Cash — but costs $100 more and doesn't have Capital One's growing lounge network. Against the CSR and Amex Platinum, the Palladium trades lounge variety for a simpler, higher flat-rate return and the unique housing angle. If you pay rent, the Palladium has an argument that nobody else can make.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• High spenders who want one premium card that earns 2x on everything without thinking about categories
  • Renters and homeowners who want premium card perks plus housing rewards — a combination only Bilt offers
  • Points maximizers who'll leverage Hyatt and airline transfers to squeeze outsized value from a flat 2x earn rate

The Palladium is Bilt's bid to be the only premium card you need. $600 in credits that exceed the $495 fee, 2x on everything, Priority Pass with two guests, and the only premium card that earns on rent. If housing is your biggest expense and you want one card to rule the rest of your spending too, this is the play.

title: Chase Freedom Unlimited
scouts_verdict: The Freedom Unlimited is the Swiss Army knife of the Chase lineup. Solo, it's a perfectly good 1.5% cash back card with a 3% kicker on dining. But pair it with a Sapphire Preferred or Reserve and it transforms — your everyday spending suddenly earns transferable points worth 2+ cents each through partners like Hyatt. The $250 bonus for just $500 in spend is easy money, and the 15-month 0% APR adds flexibility. The 3% foreign transaction fee means you need something else for international trips, but domestically? This belongs in your wallet if you're in the Chase ecosystem.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Chase Freedom Unlimited might be the most underappreciated card in the Chase ecosystem. On the surface, it's a no-annual-fee card earning 1.5% on everything, with 3% on dining and drugstores and 5% on Chase Travel portal bookings. Solid. Not flashy. But here's the thing: pair it with a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, and those "cash back" rewards transform into Ultimate Rewards points that transfer to Hyatt, United, Southwest, and more.

That dual identity — simple cash back card for casual users, transferable points engine for enthusiasts — is what makes the CFU so versatile. It also throws in a 0% intro APR for 15 months and requires exactly zero annual fees, ever. Whether you're building a Chase points strategy or just want a no-fuss card that earns well on everything, the Freedom Unlimited delivers.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 1.5% on everything: No caps, no categories to track, no quarterly activations. Just spend and earn.
  • 5% on Chase Travel: Book through the Chase portal and earn 5x. Nice bump for travel planners.
  • 3% on dining and drugstores: Restaurants, takeout, delivery, and your pharmacy runs all earn elevated rates.
  • 0% intro APR for 15 months: On both purchases and balance transfers. Useful for big buys or debt consolidation.
  • $0 annual fee: Forever. No fee creep, no strings.
  • Purchase protection: 120 days of coverage against damage or theft on new purchases.
  • Extended warranty: Adds up to one year on eligible manufacturer warranties.
  • Trip cancellation/interruption: Coverage when you book travel with the card.
  • No minimum redemption: Cash out any amount, any time.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $0

Foreign Transaction Fee: 3% of each transaction in U.S. dollars

Balance Transfer Fee: Either $5 or 3% of the amount transferred, whichever is greater (within 60 days); 5% or $5 minimum thereafter

Cash Advance Fee: Either $10 or 5% of the amount, whichever is greater

Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

The $0 fee is the headline. But that 3% foreign transaction fee is a dealbreaker for international spending — leave this one at home when you travel abroad and use something with no FTF instead.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Right now: $250 bonus after spending just $500 in the first 3 months. This limited-time offer runs March 12 through June 11, 2026, and it's $50 better than the standard $200 bonus.

$500 in 3 months is about $167 a month. Your phone bill and a few grocery trips will get you there. The card has occasionally offered bonuses as high as $300 during promo windows, so $250 is a solid middle-ground offer — not record-breaking, but easy money.

Pro tip: if you also hold a Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, that $250 in Ultimate Rewards points becomes worth more when redeemed through Chase's transfer partners. The bonus is good; the ecosystem makes it better.

sections.title: Earning Rates

No caps on any category, all rewards earned as Ultimate Rewards points (1 point = 1 cent as cash back). The 1.5% base rate is what separates this from the pack — most no-fee cards give you just 1% on non-bonus spending. That extra half percent adds up faster than you'd think when it applies to literally everything.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Points from the Freedom Unlimited can be redeemed for:

  • Cash back as a statement credit or direct deposit (1 point = 1 cent)
  • Gift cards from major retailers (generally 1 cent per point)
  • Travel through Chase Travel at 1 cent per point
  • Amazon purchases at checkout using Pay with Points

But here's the real play: hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred (1.25x through Chase Travel) or Sapphire Reserve (1.5x), and you can pool your Freedom Unlimited points with that card. Suddenly your 1.5% base rate becomes 1.875% or 2.25% when redeemed for travel. And you unlock transfers to Hyatt, United, Southwest, and more. The CFU on its own is fine. The CFU in the Chase ecosystem is genuinely excellent.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
It's a free card, so don't expect the Ritz. But the protections are surprisingly decent:

  • Trip cancellation/interruption: Up to $1,500 per person and $6,000 per trip for prepaid, non-refundable travel.
  • Auto rental CDW: Primary coverage for business rentals, secondary for personal. Not bad for a $0 card.
  • Baggage delay insurance: Covers essential purchases if bags are delayed 6+ hours.
  • Travel and emergency assistance: 24/7 hotline for medical, legal, and travel emergencies.

No lounge access, no TSA PreCheck credit, no hotel status — those are Sapphire territory. But for a card that costs nothing to hold, having trip insurance and rental car coverage is a nice touch.

sections.content:

On paper, the Double Cash and Active Cash beat the CFU with their 2% flat rate. But the CFU has two advantages they can't match: 3% on dining and drugstores (both earn more than 2% in those categories), and seamless integration with the Chase Sapphire ecosystem. If you have or plan to get a Sapphire card, the CFU's effective value blows past 2%. If you don't? A flat 2% card is probably better for pure cash back.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:
• Chase Sapphire cardholders who want the best everyday earner in the Ultimate Rewards ecosystem
  • New credit card users looking for a simple, no-fee starting point with room to grow
  • Balance transfer seekers who need 15 months of breathing room at 0% APR
  • Dining regulars who want 3% back at restaurants without paying an annual fee
  • Future points enthusiasts who want to start earning transferable points now and add a Sapphire card later

Skip this if: you travel internationally a lot (3% FTF), you just want the highest flat rate possible (get a 2% card), or you have zero interest in the Chase ecosystem. For everyone else, the Freedom Unlimited earns its wallet spot.

title: Chase Freedom Flex
scouts_verdict:
The Freedom Flex is the overachiever of the Chase family. While its sibling the Unlimited is content being reliable and boring, the Flex rewards you for paying attention — and it rewards you handsomely. Those 5% quarterly categories on Amazon, gas stations, and dining can pile up points fast if you plan around them, and the fixed 3% on dining and drugstores means even a lazy quarter isn't wasted.

But here's the benefit nobody talks about enough: the cell phone protection. Pay your phone bill with the Flex and you're covered for up to $800 in theft or damage. That's worth more than $100/year compared to carrier insurance plans, which means this "free" card is actually saving you money just by existing in your wallet. Add the $200 sign-up bonus and 0% intro APR, and the value proposition is borderline unfair for a $0 card.

The power move? Carry both the Freedom Flex and Freedom Unlimited alongside a Sapphire. The Flex handles rotating categories and dining, the Unlimited mops up everything else at 1.5%, and the Sapphire turns all those points into first-class flights and Hyatt stays. If you're only picking one Freedom card, grab the Flex if you'll activate those categories — grab the Unlimited if that sounds like homework.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Look, there are a lot of no-annual-fee cash back cards out there, but the Chase Freedom Flex is the one that keeps showing up at the top of every list — and it deserves to be there. It's built around quarterly rotating 5% cash back categories, plus fixed bonus rates on dining, drugstores, and Chase Travel. Think of it as the successor to the original Chase Freedom, now with Mastercard World Elite benefits (hello, cell phone protection) bolted on.

Here's the thing that makes the Flex special: it earns Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Pair it with a Sapphire card and suddenly those points become transferable to airlines and hotels — turning a free cash back card into a legitimate travel rewards engine. The combo of 5% rotating categories, 3% on dining, and transferable points makes this arguably the most rewarding no-fee card you can carry, as long as you don't mind setting a quarterly reminder on your phone.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 5% cash back on up to $1,500 in combined purchases in rotating bonus categories each quarter (activation required)
  • 5% cash back on travel purchased through Chase Travel
  • 3% cash back on dining (including takeout and delivery) and drugstore purchases
  • 1% cash back on all other purchases
  • No annual fee
  • 0% intro APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers
  • Mastercard World Elite benefits including cell phone protection (up to $800/claim), Mastercard ID Theft Protection, and ShopRunner membership
  • Purchase protection and extended warranty coverage

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $0

Foreign Transaction Fee: 3% of each transaction in U.S. dollars

Balance Transfer Fee: Either $5 or 3% of the amount transferred, whichever is greater (within 60 days); 5% or $5 minimum thereafter

Cash Advance Fee: Either $10 or 5% of the amount, whichever is greater

Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

The short version: no annual fee, which is awesome, but that 3% foreign transaction fee is a dealbreaker for international spending. If you're heading to Paris or Tokyo, leave this one at home and bring a no-FTF card instead. Domestically? It costs you nothing to hold forever.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn a $200 bonus after you spend $500 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is a standard, non-limited-time offer.

Spending $500 in 3 months is about as easy as a welcome bonus gets — that's a couple grocery runs and a phone bill. While the Freedom Unlimited currently has a higher limited-time $250 bonus, the Flex's $200 is always available and represents a 40% return on the required spend. Not bad for doing what you'd do anyway.

One catch to remember: Chase's 5/24 rule. If you've opened 5 or more credit cards (across all issuers) in the past 24 months, Chase will likely say no. Plan your applications accordingly.

2026 Quarterly Categories:

  • Q1 (Jan–Mar): Dining, American Heart Association donations, Norwegian Cruise Line
  • Q2 (Apr–Jun): Amazon, Whole Foods Market, Chase Travel, Feeding America donations

And here's the part people forget: you must activate each quarter's bonus at chase.com/freedom or the Chase app before making purchases. Skip activation and you're earning a sad 1% instead. Set a calendar reminder. Seriously.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
On its own, you can redeem for the usual stuff:

  • Cash back as a statement credit or direct deposit
  • Gift cards from popular retailers
  • Travel through Chase Travel portal
  • Amazon checkout via Pay with Points

But here's where the magic happens: pool your points with a Sapphire Preferred (1.25 cpp) or Sapphire Reserve (1.5 cpp) and those points get supercharged. Your 5% rotating category earnings suddenly become worth 6.25% or even 7.5% toward travel. That's elite territory for a free card.

Transfer partners include World of Hyatt, United MileagePlus, Southwest Rapid Rewards, British Airways Avios, Air France/KLM Flying Blue, and more. Hyatt transfers are the crown jewel here — you can regularly get 2+ cents per point, making those quarterly bonus categories ridiculously lucrative.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
For a card that costs zero dollars, the Freedom Flex packs a surprising amount of protection into the fine print — all thanks to its Mastercard World Elite status:

  • Cell phone protection: Up to $800 per claim ($1,000/year) when you pay your monthly cell phone bill with the card — covers theft and damage with a $50 deductible
  • Trip cancellation/interruption insurance: Up to $1,500 per person, $6,000 per trip
  • Auto rental collision damage waiver: Primary for business, secondary for personal rentals
  • Baggage delay insurance: Reimburses essentials when bags are delayed 6+ hours
  • Travel accident insurance: Up to $500,000 in coverage
  • ShopRunner membership: Free 2-day shipping at participating retailers

Let's be real — the cell phone protection alone is a game-changer. It can save you $10–15/month on carrier insurance, which means this "no-fee" card is actually making you money. That's not marketing spin; that's just math.

The Flex and Discover it are basically rivals who keep one-upping each other. Discover's first-year cashback match is genuinely hard to beat for new applicants — it's like getting a doubled welcome bonus. But long-term? The Flex wins thanks to the Chase ecosystem and that cell phone protection. If you're playing the long game, pick the Flex. If you want a wild first year, go Discover.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:

  • Chase ecosystem builders feeding Ultimate Rewards points into a Sapphire card
  • Anyone with a phone who wants free cell protection worth $100+/year
  • Amazon and Whole Foods shoppers looking to cash in big during Q2 2026
  • Two-card tacticians — the Flex + Freedom Unlimited combo covers rotating categories and flat-rate earning with zero annual fees

Skip this card if: you can't be bothered to activate categories every quarter (get the Unlimited instead), you travel internationally a lot (3% FTF says no), or you just want one simple card for everything.

title: American Express Business Gold Card
scouts_verdict:
The Business Gold is a workhorse card for businesses that spend where it counts — advertising, software, shipping, and the like. That automatic 4X on your top two categories sounds almost too clever, and honestly, it usually delivers. The catch? If your spending is scattered thinly across all six eligible categories, the 4X boost might land on amounts that don't matter much. Concentrated spending is where this card flexes.

Now, about that $375 annual fee. It looks intimidating until you stack up the credits: $240 from FedEx/Grubhub/office supplies and $155 from Walmart+ adds up to $395 — more than the fee itself. But and this is important — only count credits for services you'd actually use. Signing up for Walmart+ just to offset a credit card fee is the financial equivalent of buying something on sale you never wanted. The 100,000-point welcome bonus is excellent, though spending $15,000 in 3 months means this is truly a card for businesses with real expenses, not a side hustle.

The question that matters: Business Gold or Chase Ink Business Preferred? The Ink costs $95/year with 3X earning. The Amex costs $375 with 4X. If your business charges $50K+ annually in those bonus categories, the extra points from the Amex more than cover the fee difference. Below that threshold? The Ink Preferred and its Chase ecosystem might be the sharper play.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
If your business spends real money on ads, software, or shipping, the American Express Business Gold Card basically reads your mind. It's a charge card that earns 4X Membership Rewards points on the two categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle, automatically picked from six eligible categories. No picking, no activating — it just watches what you buy and gives you the best deal it can.

At $375/year, it sits in the sweet spot between Amex's free business cards and the premium Business Platinum. You also get 3X on flights and prepaid hotels through amextravel.com, plus a pile of statement credits that can shave the annual fee down to almost nothing — if you're the type of business that ships packages and orders lunch.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 4X Membership Rewards points on your top 2 spending categories each billing cycle from 6 eligible categories (up to $150,000/year in combined purchases, then 1X)
  • 3X points on flights and prepaid hotels booked on amextravel.com
  • 1X points on all other eligible purchases
  • $240/year in statement credits — up to $20/month for U.S. purchases at FedEx, Grubhub, and office supply stores
  • Walmart+ membership credit — monthly statement credit worth up to $155/year
  • $150 Squarespace credit — up to $150 per calendar year for eligible U.S. purchases with Squarespace (enrollment required)
  • Flexible payment: Pay Over Time feature lets you carry a balance on eligible purchases (with interest)
  • Expense management tools including Year-End Summary, Connect to QuickBooks, and employee card spending limits
  • No preset spending limit — adapts to your purchasing patterns

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $375

Additional Card Members: No additional fee

Foreign Transaction Fee: None

Late Payment Fee: Up to $40 or 2.99% of the delinquent amount, whichever is greater

Pay Over Time APR: 19.49%–27.49% variable

$375 sounds like a lot — until you do the math on the credits:

  • FedEx/Grubhub/office supply credit: up to $240/year
  • Walmart+ credit: up to $155/year

That's up to $395 in credits, which technically more than covers the annual fee. The key word is "technically" — you have to actually use these services. If you're forcing yourself to order Grubhub just to chase a $20 credit, you're doing it wrong.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 100,000 Membership Rewards points after you spend $15,000 on eligible purchases with the Business Gold Card within the first 3 months of Card Membership.

Let's be honest about that $15,000 spend requirement — it's hefty. That's $5,000/month, which means this card is calling out to businesses with real operating expenses, not someone trying to manufacture spend on gift cards. But if your business naturally drops $5K+/month on advertising, supplies, or SaaS subscriptions, you'll barely notice.

At conservative valuations (1.5–2 cents per point), 100,000 MR points are worth $1,500–$2,000 in travel. Transfer them to partners like ANA or Singapore Airlines and you can stretch that even further — business class to Tokyo, anyone?

sections.title: Earning Rates
sections.content:
The card automatically identifies your top 2 spending categories each billing cycle and applies 4X earning. No choosing, no fiddling — it just picks the two where you spent the most:

Eligible 4X CategoriesExamples
U.S. advertisingGoogle Ads, Meta Ads, LinkedIn Ads
U.S. computer hardware/software/cloudAWS, Microsoft, Adobe, Apple
U.S. gas stationsShell, ExxonMobil, BP
U.S. restaurantsAny restaurant purchase
U.S. shippingFedEx, UPS, USPS
U.S. wireless telephoneAT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile

Cap: 4X applies to the first $150,000 in combined 4X-eligible purchases per calendar year, then 1X. Additional earning: 3X on flights and prepaid hotels via amextravel.com, 1X on everything else.

The auto-selection is clever but not perfect. If your spending is spread thin across all six categories, the 4X boost might land on smaller amounts that don't really move the needle. Works best when your spending is concentrated in 2-3 categories.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Membership Rewards points are one of the most flexible currencies in the game. Here's what you can do with them:

  • Transfer to airline partners: 20+ airlines including Delta, ANA, Singapore Airlines, British Airways, Air France/KLM, JetBlue, Avianca LifeMiles, Emirates, Etihad, and more (typically 1:1 ratio)
  • Transfer to hotel partners: Hilton Honors (1:2 ratio) and Marriott Bonvoy (1:1 ratio, but less favorable)
  • Amex Travel portal: Book flights, hotels, and more at 1 cent per point (or 0.7 cpp for some redemptions)
  • Statement credits: Apply points against purchases (typically 0.6–0.7 cpp)
  • Gift cards: Variable rates, generally not the best value
  • Pay with Points at Amazon: 0.7 cpp — just don't

The money play is airline transfers, full stop. ANA first class for 80K–100K points on routes where the ticket costs $15K+? That's the kind of value that makes the annual fee look like pocket change. Singapore Airlines business class and Delta domestic awards during low-demand periods are other sweet spots worth hunting.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
Solid travel benefits here, though you won't mistake this for the Business Platinum:

  • No foreign transaction fees — good for international business spending
  • Car rental loss and damage insurance: Secondary coverage when renting for business use
  • Global Assist Hotline: 24/7 medical, legal, and travel emergency assistance
  • Travel accident insurance: Up to $100,000 in coverage
  • Baggage insurance: Up to $1,250 for carry-on, $500 for checked bags
  • Extended warranty: Adds up to one additional year on eligible purchases
  • Purchase protection: Up to $10,000 per occurrence for eligible items

What you won't find here: no airport lounge access, no airline fee credit, no hotel status, no TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit. If those are must-haves, you're looking at the Business Platinum — and an extra $320/year.

For businesses dropping serious money in the 4X categories, the Amex earns more. For everyone else, the Ink Preferred might be the smarter pick.

  • Walmart+ subscribers who'll gladly take $155/year in free membership
  • Businesses with shifting spending patterns — the auto-category selection adapts month to month

Skip this if: your monthly spend is low (that $15K bonus requirement is a signal this card wants volume), your spending is mostly international (4X categories are U.S.-only), or you need lounge access and premium travel perks baked in.

title: American Express Green Card
scouts_verdict:
The Amex Green fills an interesting niche: it's the cheapest way into Amex's Membership Rewards world, and the 3X on travel, transit, and dining covers a surprising amount of what most people spend money on. The $219 CLEAR+ credit is the swing factor that makes or breaks this card — use CLEAR and you're effectively getting paid $59/year to carry the card. That's hard to argue with.

Without CLEAR, though, the math tightens up considerably. You're paying $150/year for 3X earning and some basic protections, while the Chase Sapphire Preferred offers 3X dining, 2X travel, a $50 hotel credit, and Chase's partner network for $95. Unless you specifically need the transit category or you're chasing ANA and Singapore Airlines transfers (which are genuinely excellent), the Sapphire Preferred is the more cost-effective play for most people.

Where the Green really sings is as a supporting player in a bigger Amex lineup. Pair it with the Gold for 4X dining and groceries, let the Green handle travel and transit, and you've got your bases covered. Or keep it as your sole MR card if your spending skews heavily toward transportation. Just don't expect lounges, hotel status, or anything resembling luxury — that's Platinum territory, and Platinum money.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Think of the American Express Green Card as the entry-level ticket to the Amex Membership Rewards universe — without the premium price tag. For $150/year, you get 3X points on travel, transit, and restaurants worldwide, which is a lot of everyday spending covered at a solid rate. It sits below the Gold ($325) and Platinum ($895) in both cost and perks, and that's exactly the point.

Amex relaunched this card in 2019 after it spent years collecting dust as a forgotten product, and the new identity is clear: it's a streamlined travel-and-dining earner for people who want MR transfer partners without selling a kidney. It won't dazzle you with dining credits or grocery bonuses like the Gold, but its travel and transit earning combined with a CLEAR+ credit make it surprisingly competitive for commuters and frequent flyers.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 3X Membership Rewards points on travel worldwide (flights, hotels, car rentals, home shares)
  • 3X points on transit worldwide (taxis, rideshares, trains, buses, tolls, parking)
  • 3X points on restaurants worldwide (including takeout and delivery in the U.S.)
  • 1X points on all other eligible purchases
  • $219 CLEAR+ Credit: Annual statement credit covering a CLEAR+ membership for expedited airport security
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Car rental loss and damage insurance
  • Global Assist Hotline for travel emergencies
  • Baggage insurance plan covering lost, damaged, or stolen luggage

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $150

Additional Card Members: $35 per card

Foreign Transaction Fee: None

Late Payment Fee: Up to $40

Pay Over Time APR: 21.99%–29.99% variable

Here's the fun math: the $219 CLEAR+ credit literally exceeds the $150 annual fee. If you use CLEAR, this card pays you $69/year to hold it. That's rare. But — and this is a big but — CLEAR is only useful if you fly through airports that support it. If CLEAR isn't your thing, you're evaluating this card purely on its 3X earning structure against $150, which is a tighter call.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 40,000 Membership Rewards points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 6 months of Card Membership.

Six months to spend $3,000 is about as relaxed as welcome bonus requirements get — that's $500/month, which most people hit without trying. The 40,000 points is on the modest side, though. The card has historically offered up to 60,000 points during promotions, so it's worth checking CardMatch or Amex's pre-qualified offers before you apply. You might get lucky with a higher targeted bonus.

At 1.5–2 cents per point, 40,000 MR points are worth roughly $600–$800 toward travel. Send them to the right partner (ANA or Virgin Atlantic, for example) and you can squeeze out even more.

All 3X earning is uncapped — no limits, no quarterly activations, no nonsense. The transit category is where this card quietly shines. It covers rideshares (Uber, Lyft), subway systems, commuter rail, parking garages, tolls, and even bike-share programs. If you're commuting in a major city, your daily spend is racking up points on autopilot.

Compared to the Amex Gold (4X on dining, 4X on groceries), the Green earns less on food but more on travel and transit. If your wallet leans toward transportation rather than takeout, the Green is your card.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
You get the full Amex Membership Rewards transfer partner network — the same partners whether you hold the Green, Gold, or Platinum:

  • Airline transfers (1:1): Delta, ANA, Singapore Airlines, British Airways, Air France/KLM, JetBlue, Avianca LifeMiles, Emirates, Etihad, and more
  • Hotel transfers: Hilton Honors (1:2 ratio) and Marriott Bonvoy (1:1)
  • Amex Travel: Book at 1 cpp through the portal, or use Pay with Points
  • Statement credits: Generally 0.6–0.7 cpp (not recommended)
  • Gift cards and merchandise: Variable rates, typically poor value

The real value is in airline transfers — always. Sweet spots include ANA round-trip business class to Japan for 75,000–88,000 points, Virgin Atlantic partner awards on ANA or Delta, and Avianca LifeMiles for Star Alliance flights. Having access to this network for just $150/year is genuinely a great deal.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
Practical perks, nothing flashy — which is fine at this price:

  • $219 CLEAR+ Credit: Covers a CLEAR+ membership for expedited identity verification at airport security and select stadiums/venues. Automatically triggered when you charge CLEAR to the card.
  • No foreign transaction fees: Use freely abroad without surcharges
  • Car rental loss and damage insurance: Secondary coverage for collision damage or theft on eligible rentals
  • Baggage insurance: Up to $1,250 for carry-on, $500 for checked baggage
  • Travel accident insurance: Up to $100,000 in coverage for common carrier travel
  • Global Assist Hotline: 24/7 emergency assistance when traveling 100+ miles from home

What you won't get: no airport lounge access (no Centurion Lounges, no Priority Pass), no airline fee credit, no hotel status, no TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit. For any of that, you're upgrading to the Platinum — and its $895 fee.

sections.title: Best For

  • CLEAR members who turn the $219 credit into a card that pays them $69/year

  • International travelers who want no foreign transaction fees and worldwide 3X earning
  • Amex Gold or Platinum holders who want a dedicated transit/travel earner in their rotation

Not your card if: you spend heavily on groceries (get the Gold), you want lounge access or premium perks (you need the Platinum), or the Sapphire Preferred's $95 fee just makes more sense for your wallet.

title: Capital One Savor
scouts_verdict:
The Savor is one of those rare cards that just makes sense for almost everyone. No annual fee, no foreign transaction fees, and 3% back on the stuff you're already spending money on — restaurants, groceries, entertainment, streaming. No quarterly activation dance, no caps, no fine print gotchas. Swipe and earn.

The one real gotcha: if Walmart or Target is your grocery store, you're earning a measly 1% instead of 3%, which kind of defeats the purpose. But if you shop at actual grocery chains — Kroger, Publix, Trader Joe's, Whole Foods, Safeway — the 3% is the real deal. And the entertainment and streaming categories are a nice bonus that most competitors simply don't match.

This isn't the card for points-and-miles nerds chasing business class flights — rewards are straight cash back with no transfer partner gymnastics. But honestly, that's a feature for people who just want money back without playing a game. If you need one set-it-and-forget-it card for everyday spending, the Savor is one of the best free options out there. Pair it with a flat 2% card like the Citi Double Cash for non-bonus spending, and you've got a two-card setup that quietly crushes it.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
If you spend most of your money on eating, watching stuff, and being entertained — and let's be honest, who doesn't? — the Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card was basically built for you. It earns 3% cash back on dining, groceries, entertainment, and streaming services, which covers a huge chunk of what most households actually spend money on. Everything else earns 1%. Oh, and it's free.

Quick backstory: the current Savor is actually the rebranded former SavorOne (Capital One retired the original annual-fee Savor card in October 2024 and swapped the names). The earning structure stayed the same — straightforward and generous for a no-fee card. If you want strong cash back on food and fun without managing rotating categories or coughing up an annual fee, this is one of the best options out there.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 3% unlimited cash back on dining, including restaurants, takeout, and delivery
  • 3% unlimited cash back on grocery stores (excluding superstores like Walmart and Target)
  • 3% unlimited cash back on entertainment (movies, concerts, sporting events, amusement parks)
  • 3% unlimited cash back on popular streaming services (Netflix, Spotify, Disney+, etc.)
  • 5% cash back on hotels, vacation rentals, rental cars, and activities booked through Capital One Travel
  • 8% cash back on Capital One Entertainment purchases
  • 1% cash back on all other purchases
  • No annual fee
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Rewards never expire for the life of the account

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $0

Foreign Transaction Fee: None

Balance Transfer Fee: 3% of the transferred amount (4% for transfers within 4 months of account opening)

Cash Advance Fee: Either $10 or 3% of the amount, whichever is greater

Zero annual fee and zero foreign transaction fees — that's a combination you don't see often enough. Unlike the Chase Freedom cards (which hit you with 3% on every international purchase), the Savor works just fine in Paris or Tokyo. This is a genuinely no-cost card to own, full stop.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases within 3 months of opening your account.

$500 in 3 months is roughly $167/month — you'll probably hit it by accident. The $200 back represents a 40% return on your initial spending, which is solid for a free card. It won't make your jaw drop compared to premium travel card bonuses, but remember: there's no annual fee clawing back that value. The $200 is yours, and the 3% keeps rolling indefinitely at zero cost.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Redemption is refreshingly simple — what you earn is what you get:

  • Statement credit: Apply cash back directly against your balance (any amount)
  • Direct deposit: Transfer cash back to a bank account
  • Capital One Travel: Redeem for travel bookings at 1 cent per unit
  • Gift cards: Purchase from various retailers
  • Amazon checkout: Use rewards at Amazon.com
  • Charitable donations: Donate rewards to participating nonprofits

No transfer partners, no complicated redemption charts, no devaluation drama. One cent per cash back unit, always. Points-and-miles enthusiasts might yawn, but for everyone else, the simplicity is actually the feature. You don't need a spreadsheet to figure out what your rewards are worth.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
For a free card, you get a respectable set of extras — though don't expect anything fancy:

  • No foreign transaction fees: Use freely in any country without surcharges
  • 5% back on Capital One Travel: Hotels, vacation rentals, rental cars, and activities booked through the portal
  • 8% back on Capital One Entertainment: Concert tickets, events, and experiences purchased through Capital One's platform
  • Extended warranty: Doubles the manufacturer's warranty up to one additional year on eligible items

No trip cancellation insurance, no rental car damage waiver, no lounge access. The Savor is an everyday earning machine, not a travel fortress. If you need serious travel protections, pair it with a dedicated travel card.

title: Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant
scouts_verdict:
The Brilliant is a fantastic card — for a very specific person. If you're already loyal to Marriott and staying at their properties regularly, the value stacks up fast. Platinum Elite status is genuinely powerful at full-service Marriotts, Westins, and Sheratons where you'll score lounge access and meaningful upgrades. The 85K free night certificate can easily cover a $500+ night at a premium property. And the $300 dining credit? If you eat out even once a month, you'll use it without trying.

But let's talk about the elephant in the room: $650 is real money. If you're not disciplined about using the $25/month dining credit (use-it-or-lose-it, no rollover), and if you don't have a Ritz-Carlton or St. Regis stay planned for the property credit, you're leaving hundreds on the table. Too many people sign up for premium hotel cards thinking they'll "figure out" the credits later. Spoiler: they don't.

The bottom line: 15+ nights a year at Marriott properties plus consistent dining out? This card practically pays for itself. Under 10 nights? Save yourself $555 and grab the Boundless. And if you're on the fence, the 200K welcome bonus available through May 13, 2026 tilts the math heavily in favor of signing up now rather than later.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card is the top dog in Marriott's credit card lineup, and it comes with a price tag to match: $650/year. This is the card for people who've basically pledged their loyalty to Marriott and want the VIP treatment without having to sleep in 50+ hotel rooms a year to earn it. Think automatic Platinum Elite status, Priority Pass lounge access, and a free night certificate that can cover a seriously nice property.

Here's the deal: this card is outstanding if you're a frequent Marriott traveler who'll actually use all the credits. The dining credit, the property credit, the lounge access, the elite status perks — they add up fast when you put them to work. But if you're the type who gets a premium card and then forgets to use the benefits? That $650 will feel like a very expensive paperweight.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Automatic Platinum Elite Status — Includes room upgrades when available, late checkout, lounge access at select brands, 50% bonus points on stays, and welcome gifts.
  • Free Night Award (up to 85,000 points) — Received annually after card renewal. Can be used at properties costing up to 85K points per night, covering most Marriott hotels.
  • 25 Elite Night Credits — Applied annually toward earning or maintaining higher Marriott elite status tiers.
  • Priority Pass Select Membership — Unlimited airport lounge access for you and up to 2 guests at 1,400+ lounges worldwide.
  • $300 Annual Dining Credit — Up to $25/month in statement credits at restaurants worldwide.
  • $100 Marriott Property Credit — On qualifying 2+ night stays at Ritz-Carlton or St. Regis properties.
  • Global Entry or TSA PreCheck Credit — Statement credit of up to $85 for TSA PreCheck or $120 for Global Entry every 4 years.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees — Use the card internationally without extra charges.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $650

Foreign Transaction Fees: None

Effective Net Cost: When you factor in the free night award (worth ~$400-$600 at many properties), $300 dining credit, $100 property credit, and the value of Platinum Elite status, many cardholders can offset most or all of the annual fee. However, you need to actually use these benefits to get the value — unused credits are worth nothing.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 200,000 Marriott Bonvoy points after spending $6,000 on eligible purchases within the first 6 months of card membership. This limited-time offer is available through May 13, 2026.

Two hundred thousand points. At roughly 0.7 cents per point, that's approximately $1,400 in hotel stays — enough for multiple free nights at mid-tier properties or a couple of memorable nights at luxury Marriott brands. This is one of the strongest welcome offers in the hotel card world right now, and the $6,000 spend over 6 months ($1,000/month) is reasonable for a premium card.

title: Marriott Bonvoy Boundless
scouts_verdict:
The Boundless is quietly one of the best deals in the hotel card game, and the 2026 addition of a $100 airline credit just made it even better. At $95/year, you get a free night certificate worth $150-$250+ at most Marriott properties, plus that airline credit effectively zeroes out the fee. A hotel card that pays for itself before you earn a single point? That's the definition of a keeper card.

The earning structure is solid if unspectacular — 6x at Marriott, 3x on groceries/gas/dining with a $6,000 combined cap. Heavy spenders will hit that ceiling, but for most people it's fine. The real play here is simple: hold the card, collect your free night every year, use the airline credit, and treat any points you earn along the way as a bonus. It's low-maintenance value.

Deciding between this and the Brilliant? Ask yourself one question: do you stay at Marriott properties often enough to justify $555 more per year? If you're under 15 nights annually, the Boundless gives you the vast majority of the value at a fraction of the cost. And that 4 Free Night welcome bonus is genuinely outstanding — time a sign-up right and you could bank an entire vacation's worth of hotel stays before your first annual fee even hits.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Credit Card from Chase is the Goldilocks option in Marriott's card lineup — not too expensive, not too basic, just right for most Marriott travelers. At $95/year, it sits between the free Bold card and the premium $650 Brilliant from Amex, giving you a free night certificate, Silver Elite status, and solid earning rates without requiring you to remortgage your house.

Here's why this card keeps winning fans: you get a free night certificate every year that's typically worth $150-$250+, which more than covers the annual fee before you even start counting bonus points. It earns Marriott Bonvoy points directly (not Chase Ultimate Rewards), making it a straightforward hotel loyalty card that does exactly what it says on the tin.

  • No Foreign Transaction Fees — Use the card abroad without additional charges.
  • 4th Night Free on Award Stays — When redeeming points for 4+ consecutive nights, the 4th night is free (booked through Marriott).

Effective Net Cost: Let's do the math: a free night certificate worth $150-$250+ at most Marriott properties, plus a new $100 airline credit for 2026. That's $250-$350+ in tangible value against a $95 fee. This card can be net positive before you even earn a single point. In the hotel card world, that kind of math is rare — and it makes the Boundless one of the easiest keeper cards to justify.

That's up to 4 Free Night Awards total, each valid at properties costing up to 50,000 points per night. At mid-range Marriott hotels, this can easily represent $800-$1,200+ in hotel value. Here's the thing about free night certificates: they work on high-demand dates when cash rates are inflated, which means they're often worth more than you'd expect. Time this right and you could fund an entire long-weekend getaway.

title: Marriott Bonvoy Bold
scouts_verdict:
Nobody is going to brag about the Marriott Bonvoy Bold at a dinner party. It's not that kind of card. It's the kind of card you toss in your wallet because it costs nothing and quietly gives you something back — Silver Elite status, a handful of night credits, 2x on groceries and streaming, and a free DashPass. Modest? Sure. But free is a powerful price.

The refreshed 2x categories (rideshare, food delivery, streaming, phone bills) make it more useful day-to-day than the old version, but that 1x base rate means you should only reach for this card in bonus categories and at Marriott hotels. For everything else, a 2% cash back card will serve you better.

Here's who should actually get the Bold: someone who stays at Marriott a few times a year, wants to passively accumulate points, and would rather not think about annual fees. It's also a great sidekick if you already have the Boundless or Brilliant — use the Bold for 2x everyday categories and the premium card for hotel bookings. The 30K welcome bonus is modest, but with only $1,000 to spend, it's basically a free $200 hotel weekend for minimal effort.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Let's be real: the Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card from Chase isn't going to make anyone's heart race. It's the entry-level Marriott card, and its biggest selling point is dead simple — it's free. No annual fee, no drama. It's for people who stay at Marriott a few times a year and want to accumulate some points without paying for the privilege.

It doesn't have the free night certificate of the Boundless or the Platinum Elite status of the Brilliant. What it does have is automatic Silver Elite status, a surprisingly broad set of 2x earning categories (refreshed in 2024-2025 to include rideshare, streaming, and food delivery), and a complimentary DashPass membership. Think of it less as a credit card to get excited about and more as a smart, zero-cost tool to keep in your wallet.

  • No Foreign Transaction Fees — Use the card internationally without surcharges.
  • Complimentary DashPass (12 months) — Free DashPass membership for DoorDash and Caviar when activated (available through 12/31/2027), providing $0 delivery fees on eligible orders.
  • Points Redemption for Travel Credit — Redeem Bonvoy points as statement credits for qualifying airline or Marriott hotel purchases, up to $750/year.

You won't get a free night certificate like the Boundless or Brilliant, but you also won't pay a cent to hold this card. It's an excellent "sock drawer" card for maintaining Silver Elite status at zero cost — or a solid companion to a premium Marriott card for everyday 2x spending.

Earn 30,000 Marriott Bonvoy points after spending $1,000 on eligible purchases within the first 3 months of account opening.

Let's not sugarcoat it — 30,000 points isn't going to get you a suite at the St. Regis. But it's enough for 1-2 nights at a Category 1-3 Marriott (think Courtyard, Fairfield, Four Points). At a typical valuation of 0.7 cents per point, that's roughly $210 in hotel value. For a free card with a $1,000 spend requirement, that's essentially a free hotel weekend for doing your normal shopping.

title: Wells Fargo Active Cash
scouts_verdict:
The Active Cash is the answer to the question: \"What if a credit card just... worked?\" Two percent back on everything, no annual fee, no categories to remember, no quarterly activation rituals. In a world full of cards trying to be clever, this one is content to be straightforward — and it's better for it.

What pushes it past other flat-rate cards is the stuff you don't expect at $0/year. Cell phone protection covering up to $600 per claim? That's a benefit that normally lives behind a $95+ annual fee. Visa Signature perks like the Luxury Hotel Collection and 24/7 concierge are genuine bonuses, not the kind of filler benefits that sound nice on paper but mean nothing in practice. And if you pair this with a Wells Fargo Autograph, you unlock transfer partners — turning a simple cash back card into part of a real points strategy.

The only real weakness: that 3% foreign transaction fee means this card needs to stay home when you fly overseas. But for everything domestic — groceries, gas, bills, subscriptions, the random impulse buy at 11 PM — this is as good as it gets for free. It's not exciting, and that's exactly why it works.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Some cards try to impress you with complicated category structures and rotating bonuses. The Wells Fargo Active Cash Card takes the opposite approach: 2% cash back on everything, no annual fee, end of story. No categories to track, no bonuses to activate, no spending caps. Just a flat, unlimited 2% on every single purchase you make. It's the sweatpants of credit cards — not flashy, but comfortable and effective.

Since its launch, the Active Cash has been a top-tier pick for anyone who values simplicity. And in 2026, it still holds up as one of the best flat-rate cash back cards in the U.S., backed by Visa Signature benefits that include some surprisingly premium perks for a free card.

• Unlimited 2% cash rewards on all purchases — no categories, no caps
  • $0 annual fee — free to hold indefinitely
  • 0% intro APR for 12 months on purchases from account opening
  • Cell phone protection — up to $600 per claim ($25 deductible) when you pay your phone bill with the card; covers theft and damage, up to 2 claims per 12 months
  • Visa Signature Concierge — 24/7 concierge for dining, travel, and event bookings
  • Visa Signature Luxury Hotel Collection — room upgrades, free Wi-Fi, complimentary breakfast, and late checkout at select hotels
  • No expiring rewards — points stay as long as the account is open
  • Roadside dispatch via Visa Signature

title: Wells Fargo Autograph
scouts_verdict:
The Wells Fargo Autograph is quietly one of the best no-annual-fee cards you can get, and it flies under the radar compared to flashier options. Six categories at 3x, no foreign transaction fees, and direct access to transfer partners — all for $0/year. Most cards offering this kind of flexibility charge $95 to $250 annually. The Autograph just hands it over and doesn't ask for anything back.

The transfer partners are the headline act. British Airways, Virgin Atlantic, Air France/KLM, JetBlue — all at 1:1 ratios with no minimums. A well-timed transfer to British Airways for a short-haul award or Virgin Atlantic for a premium cabin seat can easily get you 1.5 to 2+ cents per point. And unlike the Chase Freedom Flex, you don't need a $550 Sapphire Reserve lurking in the background to make transfers happen.

The ultimate move? Pair the Autograph with the Active Cash. Use the Autograph for its 3x categories, the Active Cash for everything else at 2%, pool the points, and transfer to partners. Boom — you have a powerhouse rewards system with a combined annual fee of exactly zero dollars. Try to beat that.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Here's a card that punches way above its weight class: the Wells Fargo Autograph Card earns 3x points across six spending categories — restaurants, travel, gas stations, EV charging, transit, streaming services, and phone plans — plus 1x on everything else. And the kicker? No annual fee. Oh, and it comes with transfer partners. For free. That's the kind of combination that used to require a $95+ annual fee card.

It's no surprise this was named The Points Guy's No-Annual-Fee Card of the Year for 2026. The Autograph has become a go-to for rewards enthusiasts who want category bonuses and the ability to transfer to airlines and hotels — without paying for the privilege. It's the card that made people realize you don't always have to spend money to earn points the smart way.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 3x points per dollar on restaurants, travel, gas, EV charging, transit, streaming, and phone plans
  • 1x points per dollar on all other purchases
  • $0 annual fee
  • No foreign transaction fees — great for international travel
  • Airline and hotel transfer partners — 8 partners with 1:1 transfer ratios (except Choice Hotels at 1:2)
  • Cell phone protection — up to $600 per claim ($25 deductible) when paying your phone bill with the card
  • 0% intro APR for 12 months on purchases
  • No minimum transfer amount — transfer as few as 1 point to partners

Read that fee column again: $0 annual fee and $0 foreign transaction fees. You can carry this card internationally, use it every day at home, and it never costs you a dime. That's a rare double-zero that even some $95/year cards can't match.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 in purchases in the first 3 months of account opening. That's worth $200 in cash redemption value — or potentially more when transferred to airline partners.

$1,000 in 3 months is manageable for just about anyone with normal spending habits. And while $200 isn't a jaw-dropping bonus, remember: you're not paying an annual fee, so every cent of that bonus is pure profit.

Six bonus categories at 3x with no annual fee — look around, you won't find another card doing this. And these aren't obscure niche categories either. Restaurants, gas, travel, transit, streaming, phone plans — that's literally where most people spend most of their money. You don't have to change your habits to earn well with this card; your habits are already the bonus categories.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
This is where the Autograph gets really interesting for a free card:

  • Transfer to airline/hotel partners at 1:1 ratios (1:2 for Choice Hotels) — this is where the real value lives
  • Book travel through the Wells Fargo rewards portal at 1 cent per point
  • Statement credits applied to your balance
  • Gift cards from select retailers
  • Direct deposit to a Wells Fargo account

Transferring to partners is the power move. British Airways short-haul awards, Virgin Atlantic premium cabin seats, Air France/KLM deals — these can easily yield 1.5 to 2+ cents per point. Most cards with transfer partner access charge you $95-$250/year for the privilege. This one? Free.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
No travel credits or lounge access — but the travel-oriented perks are genuinely useful:

  • No foreign transaction fees — use freely abroad without extra charges
  • 8 transfer partners including:
    • Air France/KLM Flying Blue (1:1)
    • British Airways Executive Club (1:1)
    • Virgin Atlantic Flying Club (1:1)
    • Aer Lingus AerClub (1:1)
    • Avianca LifeMiles (1:1)
    • JetBlue TrueBlue (1:1)
    • Iberia Plus (1:1)
    • Choice Privileges (1:2)
  • Cell phone protection — up to $600 per claim when you pay your phone bill with the card

The transfer partner list keeps expanding, and with 1:1 ratios and no minimum transfer amounts, the flexibility here is real. You're getting the kind of redemption power that used to be reserved for premium cardholders.

The Chase Freedom Flex needs a Sapphire card ($95-$550) to unlock transfers. The SavorOne has no transfer option at all. The Autograph just gives it to you. For free. It's honestly a little wild.

sections.title: Best For
sections.content:

  • Frequent diners and travelers whose spending naturally falls into the 3x categories
  • International travelers who need a no-FTF, no-AF card that can do everything
  • Daily commuters racking up spending on gas, transit, and rideshares
  • Subscription stacking streamers with Netflix, Spotify, Disney+, and more

Not ideal if: you want the absolute highest flat-rate return on everything (the Active Cash's 2% beats the Autograph's 1x on non-category spend) or you're chasing premium lounge access.

title: Discover it Cash Back
scouts_verdict:
The Discover it Cash Back is the most underrated card in America. In an era of flashy travel cards with $695 annual fees, a free card that effectively gives you 10% cash back in bonus categories for an entire year is borderline absurd. The Cashback Match is the single best first-year offer in the credit card industry — automatic, unlimited, and no-strings-attached. Nobody else is doing this. Nobody.

After year one, the card settles into a reliable 5%-on-rotating-categories, 1%-on-everything-else rhythm. That's good but not dominant. The real strategy is pairing it correctly: use the Discover for 5% categories, a flat 2% card for everything else, and you've built a no-fee reward system that rivals cards with annual fees. The quarterly activation takes 30 seconds and is only mildly annoying.

The knock on Discover is the network. Domestically you're fine — most merchants take it. Internationally and at some smaller businesses, you'll occasionally get turned away. Never carry this as your only card. But as part of a multi-card strategy, especially in your first year, the Discover it Cash Back is almost impossible to outvalue on pure math. Get it, maximize year one, and keep it forever.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Discover it Cash Back has a party trick that no other card can match: Cashback Match. Discover literally doubles every cent of cash back you earn in your entire first year — no caps, no catches, no fine print gotchas. That means the 5% rotating quarterly categories effectively become 10%, and the base 1% becomes 2%. For 12 full months. It's the kind of offer that makes you wonder what Discover knows that other issuers don't.

Beyond the first-year fireworks, this is a solid no-annual-fee card with rotating 5% bonus categories and 1% on everything else, running on the Discover network. That network is the one caveat — it's accepted at most U.S. merchants but notably weaker internationally. Still, as a domestic cash back card and especially as a first credit card, the Discover it is extremely hard to beat.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• 5% Cash Back on Rotating Categories — Earn 5% back on up to $1,500 in purchases per quarter in rotating bonus categories (activation required each quarter).
  • 1% Cash Back on Everything Else — Flat 1% on all non-bonus purchases.
  • Cashback Match (First Year) — Discover automatically matches ALL cash back earned at the end of your first year. Unlimited, no minimum, no sign-up required.
  • $0 Annual Fee — No annual fee, ever.
  • 0% Intro APR — 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 15 months (then 17.49%-26.49% variable).
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees — Unusual for a no-fee card, making it usable abroad.
  • Free FICO Score — Access your FICO credit score online and on monthly statements.
  • Cash Back Never Expires — Rewards don't expire for the life of the account.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $0

Foreign Transaction Fees: None

Late Payment Fee: Up to $41

Balance Transfer Fee: 3% intro fee for the first 15 months, then 5%

Effective Net Cost: Absolutely nothing. This card is free to own, and the rotating categories plus first-year match deliver genuine value without you spending a single dollar on fees. There's no reason not to keep this card open long-term — even if you only pull it out for bonus category quarters, it's earning money for you.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
The Discover it Cash Back doesn't do a traditional sign-up bonus — it does something better. The Cashback Match means Discover matches 100% of all cash back you earn during your entire first year.

Think of it as an unlimited, uncapped welcome bonus that grows with how much you use the card. Max out the 5% categories ($1,500/quarter x 4 = $6,000 at 5%) and spend moderately elsewhere, and a typical first-year haul is $300-$500 in cash back, doubled to $600-$1,000 after the match. The average cardholder earns roughly $525 in matched cash back. No other no-annual-fee card comes anywhere close to that kind of first-year value. Not even in the same zip code.

  • Q1 (Jan-Mar): Grocery stores, wholesale clubs, select streaming services

Don't forget: You must activate the 5% categories each quarter through your Discover account. It doesn't apply retroactively, so any purchases you make before activation earn just 1%. Takes 30 seconds online — set a calendar reminder for the 1st of January, April, July, and October.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
Discover keeps things beautifully simple:

  • Statement Credits — Apply cash back as a credit to your account balance. Available in any amount.
  • Direct Deposit — Transfer cash back directly to your bank account.
  • Gift Cards — Redeem for gift cards from popular retailers, sometimes at a discount (e.g., $20 in cash back for a $25 gift card to select merchants).
  • Amazon Checkout — Use cash back directly at Amazon.com at checkout (1:1 value).
  • PayPal — Transfer cash back to your PayPal account.
  • Charitable Donations — Donate cash back to select charities.

No transfer partners, no complicated redemption charts, no devaluation anxiety. Cash back is always worth face value — a dollar is a dollar. The gift card discounts are actually a nice perk where you can sometimes get an extra 25% by converting to select retailers.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
Let's be honest — this is not a travel card, and it doesn't pretend to be. But it does have a few useful features for travelers:

  • No Foreign Transaction Fees: A rare perk for a no-annual-fee card. You can use it abroad without extra charges, though Discover network acceptance is limited outside the US.
  • Free FICO Score: Handy for monitoring credit health, especially if you're building toward a premium travel card application.
  • Secondary Car Rental Coverage: Discover provides secondary collision damage coverage when you rent a car and decline the rental company's insurance.

What's missing: No travel insurance, no trip delay/cancellation coverage, no purchase protection, no lounge access. If travel perks matter, pair this with a dedicated travel card and use the Discover purely for cash back.

  • Low-maintenance savers who want a no-fee, no-fuss card they can keep open forever
  • Occasional international travelers who appreciate no foreign transaction fees (just check that merchants accept Discover first)

Not the card for: people who want a flat 2% on everything (get the Citi Double Cash or Wells Fargo Active Cash), frequent travelers who need travel protections, or anyone who'll forget to activate quarterly categories and lose out on 5%.

title: IHG One Rewards Premier
scouts_verdict:
Here's the bottom line: the IHG Premier is the most underrated hotel card on the market. Full stop. You're getting Platinum Elite status for $99 — the same tier competitors charge $550-$650 to hand out. Sure, IHG's Platinum isn't going to get you upgraded to a palace suite, but it's real status with real perks at a fraction of the price.

The earning structure is sneaky good, too. That 3x on everything means this card actually works as a daily driver, not just a hotel card you dust off for travel. Most hotel cards give you 1-2x on everyday spending, so 3x is doing real work. And at IHG properties, stacking bonuses push you to 26x per dollar — those points pile up fast on a multi-night stay.

Let's be honest about the downsides: IHG points are worth less per point than Marriott or Hyatt, and a Holiday Inn Express isn't exactly a Ritz-Carlton. But if you travel frequently, stay at IHG properties even once or twice a year, and want a card that over-delivers for under $100, the Premier is a no-brainer. The 140K welcome bonus is strong enough to fund a week-long vacation on points alone. For $99, that's kind of ridiculous.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Look, most hotel credit cards at the $99 price point give you a participation trophy and call it "status." The IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card from Chase actually gives you Platinum Elite status — the real deal, with room upgrades, late checkout, and welcome amenities. For a card that costs less than dinner for two at a nice restaurant, that's kind of absurd.

IHG's portfolio spans over 6,000 properties across 100+ countries — we're talking InterContinental, Kimpton, Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza, Hotel Indigo, and more. The card pairs that Platinum Elite status with an anniversary free night certificate, a 4th Night Free benefit on award stays, and earning rates that quietly embarrass cards costing three times as much. If you stay at IHG properties even occasionally, this card is punching way above its weight class.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• Automatic Platinum Elite Status — Room upgrades when available, welcome amenity, extended checkout, bonus points on stays, and complimentary internet. No qualifying nights required — just open the card.
  • Anniversary Free Night Award — Shows up every year after your card anniversary, good at properties costing up to 40,000 points per night. This alone can be worth more than the annual fee.
  • 4th Night Free on Award Stays — Redeeming points for 4+ consecutive nights? The 4th night is on the house. That's a built-in 25% discount on longer stays.
  • $50 United TravelBank Cash — Annual credit after registering your card with your MileagePlus account. Free money for flights.
  • Global Entry/TSA PreCheck Credit — Up to $120 every 4 years for the application fee. Skip the security line on IHG's dime.
  • Complimentary DashPass — 1-year membership for DoorDash/Caviar with $0 delivery fees on eligible orders.
  • No Foreign Transaction Fees — Use it worldwide without the surcharge tax.
  • $100 Statement Credit + 10K Bonus Points — Hit $20,000+ in spending in a calendar year and get rewarded for the loyalty.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $99

Foreign Transaction Fees: None

The real math: The free night certificate alone (up to 40K points, worth $100-$200+ at most IHG properties) covers the annual fee. Toss in the $50 United TravelBank credit and Platinum Elite status, and you're looking at $200-$400+ in annual value for just $99. That's not marketing spin — the value-to-cost ratio here is genuinely one of the best in the hotel card space. It's almost hard to lose money on this card.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 140,000 IHG One Rewards bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening.

Here's the thing about IHG points: they're worth roughly 0.5-0.6 cents each, so this bonus clocks in at approximately $700-$840 in hotel value. That's enough for 3-4 nights at mid-range IHG properties or 1-2 nights at premium InterContinental or Kimpton hotels. And because of the 4th Night Free benefit, longer stays stretch that welcome bonus even further. Not bad for a $99 card.

Let's be real — these earning rates are quietly ridiculous. That 3x base rate on everything else? Most hotel cards give you 1-2x on non-category spending. IHG gives you 3x on your electric bill, your Amazon order, your random Target run. And at IHG properties, the bonuses stack like a layer cake: 10x card bonus + 10x base member earning + 6x Platinum Elite bonus = up to 26x total points per dollar. That adds up fast on a multi-night stay.

sections.title: Redemption Options
sections.content:
IHG One Rewards points can be redeemed across their global hotel portfolio — and some options are better than others:

  • Free Night Stays — The main event. Book at 6,000+ IHG properties worldwide. Dynamic pricing means rates vary by property and date, typically ranging from 10,000-70,000+ points per night.
  • Points + Cash — Combine points with a cash co-pay when you're short on points. Handy, not thrilling.
  • 4th Night Free — Book 4+ consecutive nights on points and night four is complimentary. That's a straight 25% discount on longer award stays. Use this.
  • Airline Transfers — You can transfer points to select airline partners, but the rates are terrible. Just don't.
  • Gift Cards & Merchandise — Available through the IHG rewards catalog. Also terrible value. Stick with hotel stays.

sections.title: Travel Credits & Perks
sections.content:
• $50 United TravelBank Cash: Earn up to $50 annually after registering your IHG Premier card with your MileagePlus account. Basically a free short-haul flight discount every year.
  • Platinum Elite Status: Automatic enrollment in IHG's second-highest tier. Room upgrades (when available), welcome amenity/bonus points, extended checkout, priority check-in, and complimentary internet. Cards charging $550+ offer comparable status — you're getting it for $99.
  • Global Entry/TSA PreCheck: Up to $120 statement credit every 4 years for the application fee — one of the higher reimbursement amounts among hotel cards.
  • DashPass Membership: Complimentary 1-year DashPass for DoorDash and Caviar with $0 delivery fees. A nice cherry on top.
  • $100 Milestone Credit: Earn a $100 statement credit plus 10,000 bonus points in any calendar year you spend $20,000+ on the card.

But dollar-for-dollar value at this price point, the Premier is the card to beat.

sections.title: Best For

• IHG loyalists who regularly stay at Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza, InterContinental, Kimpton, or other IHG brands.

  • Travelers booking longer stays who can leverage the 4th Night Free benefit to shave 25% off award redemptions.
  • United Airlines flyers who can pocket the $50 United TravelBank credit annually.
  • Everyday spenders who appreciate that 3x base rate pulling its weight on every purchase.

The short version on who should skip it: travelers who rarely stay at IHG properties, luxury hotel snobs (IHG's luxury portfolio is smaller than Marriott's or Hilton's), or anyone who'd rather earn transferable points than hotel-specific ones.

title: Delta SkyMiles Gold
scouts_verdict:
The Delta Gold is the no-brainer entry point for anyone who flies Delta even a few times a year. The math is dead simple: two round trips with a checked bag saves you $140, nearly covering the $150 annual fee — and year one is free, so you're playing with house money from day one.

Stack on the 2X earning at restaurants and supermarkets, and you've got a card that works for you between trips, not just at the airport. The $200 Delta flight credit after $10K in spending is a nice reward for loyalty, and the current sign-up bonus of up to 90,000 miles is one of the richest in the entry-level airline card space — enough for a domestic round-trip or a one-way to Europe.

The honest trade-off: no companion certificate (that's the Platinum), no Sky Club access (that's the Reserve), and 1X on everything outside Delta, dining, and groceries is pretty meh. If you're a hardcore Delta loyalist flying every week, you should probably upgrade. But for the person who flies Delta a handful of times a year and wants solid value without overthinking it? The Gold nails it.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Delta SkyMiles Gold American Express Card is where most people start their Delta credit card journey, and honestly? For a lot of flyers, it's where they should stay. At $150 per year ($0 for the first year), it covers the essentials — free checked bag, 2X miles on dining and groceries, priority boarding — without asking you to shell out for perks you'll never use.

Think of the Gold card as the sensible sedan of the Delta lineup. It won't turn heads, but it'll get you where you need to go and save you money doing it. The $200 Delta flight credit (after $10,000 in spending) is a nice kicker, and the current sign-up bonus of up to 90,000 miles is genuinely generous for a card at this price. No companion cert, no lounge access — just solid, no-fuss value for the occasional-to-moderate Delta flyer.

sections.title: Key Benefits
sections.content:
• First checked bag free on Delta flights for the cardholder — saves $35 each way, $70 per round trip. Two trips and the card nearly pays for itself.
  • $200 Delta Flight Credit after spending $10,000 on the card in a calendar year — not automatic, but worth chasing if you're close.
  • 15% off Delta Award Travel when redeeming SkyMiles for flights. Like a built-in coupon for every award booking.
  • Priority boarding on Delta flights — board before the main cabin masses.
  • No foreign transaction fees
  • Uber One membership credit — up to $9.99/month statement credit for Uber One membership for up to 6 consecutive months (through June 25, 2026)
  • $100 Delta Stays Credit — up to $100 in statement credits each calendar year for prepaid hotels or vacation rentals booked through Delta Stays on delta.com.
  • 20% back on Delta in-flight purchases — food, beverages, headsets. Wi-Fi excluded, sadly.

sections.title: Annual Fee & Costs
sections.content:
Annual Fee: $0 introductory for the first year, then $150 per year.

Foreign Transaction Fees: None.

Other Fees: Standard Amex fee schedule applies — late payment fee up to $40, cash advance fee of $10 or 5% (whichever is greater), and balance transfer fee of $5 or 3%.

Here's the napkin math: two round trips with a checked bag saves you $140, which nearly covers the $150 fee. Hit the $10K spending threshold and the $200 flight credit makes you come out way ahead. And year one is free, so you're literally playing with house money.

sections.title: Sign-up Bonus
sections.content:
Earn 70,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 6 months of card membership, plus an additional 20,000 bonus SkyMiles after spending an additional $2,000 in the first 6 months — for a total of 90,000 miles after $5,000 in spending.

At an approximate valuation of 1.2 cents per SkyMile, this welcome bonus is worth roughly $1,080. For a $150 card with the first year free, that's an outstanding return. We're talking enough miles for a round-trip domestic flight or even a one-way to Europe in economy. Don't sleep on this one.
